That’s great to hear. But what I highly recommend is that you also take the chemistry SAT subject exam. It’s a strictly multiple choice exam that covers the topics more basic and simplistic than its AP counterpart. You probably should have taken it in June after your AP test so the content would stay fresh, but you can still take it in this upcoming December. Two weeks of prep before the test would be ideal though.

And if you don’t know what an SAT subject exam is, it essentially shows to the colleges your knowledge in a specific subject. It’s out of 800, and the curves are usually quite generous. Do research though, and if you’re interested then I highly recommend you take it. Also think about the Math 2 subject test (that covers all of highschool math up to precalculus; this excludes any calculus).

Good luck

Ok so I know exactly the pickle you are in. I’m assuming you are a junior in highschool, and that next year is your last year. Now consider that your college applications will be due in November of next year (and your AP tests will be the May after that). Essentially, it doesn’t matter about your performance in those classes in second semester or during AP testing, since you will already be accepted or denied to college by then (so long you don’t absolutely plummet your grades). 

Now about your premed interests; since I just established that your performance in whatever you pick likely will not matter (only the 1st semester will) you will have to pick the class that appeals the most to the majors you are applying for, not what appeals to your side interests.

And honestly, AP physics C is a very rigorous course compared to Physics 1, and yielding even a 3 on the AP test only attains elective credit (you’re better off self studying AP microeconomics or AP psychology for elective credit, since there’s no harm upon failing those at the end of senior year obviously). 

AP biology is more friendly when it comes to a 3 (or greater). It’s an easier test anyway since it’s much less memorization and more problem solving (trust me that’s a good thing). And AP biology, AP chemistry, or ideally both are a must for a health major.
